newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire government raises stakes in bank note dispute.
newsitem.headline: Zaire government raises stakes in bank note dispute.

text.p: Zaire's government has hit back at opponents of new larger denomination bank notes, saying any statements against their use will be treated as a threat to national security.
The new notes -- in denominations of 100,000, of 500,000 and one of million new zaires -- were issued on January 6 but have been widely rejected by the population at large.

In his account of the weekly cabinet meeting, broadcast by state television late on Friday, government spokesman Koloni Longo said any public declaration against Central Bank monetary policy would be treated as a threat to national security.

"Article 109 of the transitional constitution names the Bank of Zaire as the monetary authority. Consequently public declarations concerning the release of new bank bills, threaten the sovereignty and security of the state," Koloni said.
"The government calls on the relevant judicial authorities to act on competent jurisdiction conforming to articles...of the penal code," he added.

The issue of new banknotes during a period of galloping inflation in 1992 led to widespread looting by soldiers after the radical opposition rejected the bills as worthless pieces of paper. Soldiers were initially paid in the new bills.
Members of the radical opposition allied to Etienne Tshisekedi called for a total boycott of the latest notes after the government announced their imminent release two weeks ago.

Other powerful personalities and groups have joined a chorus of criticism of government monetary policy, including Bemba Saolona, president of the Zaire business association, ANEZA, and a former financial advisor to President Mobutu Sese Seko.
Bemba, a political foe of Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo, has been conducting a media campaign against the notes in local newspapers and on independent Zairean television.
He says the notes have fuelled inflation and will have dire consequences for the general population and business community.

A boycott of the notes has been widely followed in Kinshasa's sprawling shanty towns and markets, where Tshisekedi draws his support. International hotels, supermarkets and many petrol service stations have begun refusing to accept them.

Zaire's main human rights group, AZADHO, has urged government to withdraw the notes but the government on Friday denounced the boycott as political, saying politicians had hijacked the issue to further personal ambitions.

The Central Bank says the notes are necessary to keep pace with inflation which had forced people to carry round huge wads of notes to pay for even the most basic purchases. It says printing smaller denomination notes has become uneconomical.
Critics say the new notes are inflationary. Prices of some basic commodities more than doubled after the government announced its plan to issue them.

Further protests over the new notes would complicate a national crisis over a rebellion in eastern Zaire by Rwandan-backed rebels who have seized territory. Retreating Zaire soldiers are already pillaging towns on their route.
Torrential rains forced the radical opposition to abandon plans for a protest march on Friday.
